We have proton NMR data: peaks at 2.58 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 2.84 (t, J=7.4, 2H), 3.81 (s, 3H), aromatic doublets: 7.17 (ddd, 2H) and 7.93 (ddd, 2H). This suggests a para-disubstituted aromatic ring with two sets of equivalent protons (AA'BB'). The aromatic pattern suggests electron-withdrawing and electron-donating substituents? Chemical shifts: 7.17 and 7.93, typical for anisole (methoxy) vs carbonyl? The 3.81 s (3H) is a methoxy group attached to aromatic O (anisole). The aliphatic signals: two triplets each 2H at 2.58 and 2.84, J=7.4, suggests -CH2-CH2- chain. Likely an ethyl ester: O-CH2-CH2-? Actually typical ethyl acetate: CH3CH2O- gives quartet and triplet. Here we have two triplets, meaning CH2-CH2 both attached to heteroatoms? Could be -CH2-CH2- between aromatic and carbonyl: e.g., phenoxyacetate? Let's think: COc1ccc(cc1) is anisole ring (methoxy phenyl). Then we have -CH2-CH2- attached to carbonyl? The pattern: 2.58 (t) and 2.84 (t). If we have -O-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-OCH3? Actually methyl ester of phenoxyacetic acid? Let's propose structure: anisole (para?) Wait the aromatic pattern is AA'BB' suggests para substitution. The methoxy group is likely para to the side chain. So the ring is 4-methoxyphenyl attached to -CH2-CH2-COOCH3? That would be 4-methoxyphenethyl acetate? Actually 4-methoxyphenethyl acetate: anisole ring with ethyl chain attached to carbonyl? Let's draw: 4-methoxyphenyl-CH2-CH2-O-COCH3? No, acetate of phenethyl alcohol: phenethyl acetate: phenyl-CH2-CH2-O-COCH3. In that case aromatic protons would be unsubstituted phenyl (multiplet). Not AA'BB'.

If para substitution: 4-methoxyphenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3 (para-methoxy phenylacetic acid methyl ester with extra CH2?). Actually phenylacetic acid methyl ester is Ph-CH2-COOCH3, aromatic pattern is monosubstituted phenyl (complex). Not AA'BB'.

Para-disubstituted aromatic with methoxy and carbonyl side chain (like para-methoxy phenylacetyl?). For para-methoxy phenylacetyl chloride? The side chain is -CH2-COOCH3? That would give CH2 (singlet?) Actually CH2 attached to aromatic and carbonyl: Ph-CH2-COOCH3 gives CH2 as singlet? No, CH2 attached to aromatic (sp2) and carbonyl, not coupled to other protons, appears as singlet around 3.5. Not observed.

Our data shows two CH2 triplets, meaning -CH2-CH2- chain between aromatic and carbonyl. So aromatic attached to CH2 (next to aromatic) which couples to next CH2 (triplet). So structure: aromatic-CH2-CH2-COOCH3. Aromatic is para-methoxy substituted. So overall: 4-methoxyphenyl-CH2-CH2-COOCH3. That matches: aromatic AA'BB' (para). Methoxy on ring (3.81 s). Two CH2 triplets (2.58 and 2.84). Methyl ester OCH3? Wait we have OCH3 as part of ester (methyl). That would appear as singlet around 3.7-3.9 as well, but we already have a singlet at 3.81 (3H). Could be the methyl of ester, not the aromatic methoxy. But aromatic methoxy also 3H singlet ~3.8. Which one is present? Could be both? But only one singlet observed. So only one OCH3 present. So either aromatic methoxy or ester methyl, not both. Which is more likely? The aromatic protons shift: 7.17 and 7.93. For anisole (para-methoxy) the aromatic protons appear around 6.8-7.2. For para-acetoxy phenyl? Not sure. If the OCH3 is the methyl of ester, the aromatic is unsubstituted phenyl (monosubstituted) giving multiplet not AA'BB'. So must be para-disubstituted aromatic with one substituent being OCH3 (methoxy) and the other being the ethyl carbonyl chain. Then we have only one OCH3 (the aromatic methoxy). The ester methyl is missing? Wait the carbonyl is part of an ester: -COOCH3? That would have methyl. But maybe it's a carboxylic acid (COOH) not ester. Then no methyl. The carbonyl could be a ketone: -CH2-CH2-CO-? But then we need something else. The data shows only one singlet 3H, likely aromatic methoxy. So the carbonyl is likely a ketone (no OCH3). So structure: 4-methoxyphenyl-CH2-CH2-CO-? But need something attached to carbonyl, maybe a methyl (acetyl). That would be -COCH3, giving a methyl singlet around 2.1, not observed. So maybe carbonyl is part of an aldehyde? That would give aldehyde ~9-10 ppm, not present. So maybe carbonyl is part of a carboxylic acid (COOH) which may not show in 1H NMR (broad). Could be.

Thus plausible structure: 4-methoxyphenylacetic acid? No chain length.

Our chain is CH2-CH2-COOH (phenethylacetic acid). That would have two CH2 triplets (adjacent). Aromatic para-methoxy. So final SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)O. Wait that is 4-methoxyphenylacetic acid (CH2-COOH). That's only one CH2. Not correct.

We need CH2-CH2-COOH: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)O? That's same: phenyl-CH2-CH2-COOH? Actually COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)O has aromatic attached to CH2-CH2-COOH (two CH2). Yes: aromatic-CH2-CH2-COOH. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)O. That matches: aromatic methoxy, para substitution, chain of two CH2, carboxylic acid. The acid proton may be exchangeable, not seen. So 1H NMR would have two triplets (J~7) for CH2s, aromatic AA'BB', methoxy singlet. Good.

Thus answer SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CC(=O)O.

We should validate? Already validated earlier a similar but with ester. Let's validate this new SMILES.
